utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Petrovic, you've got until 10.00. Please proceed. But before you do so, Mr. Milovanovic, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic will now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 5604. In B/C/S it's page 77. In English it's page 79. English 79, B/C/S copy 77. The handwritten version also page 77. We have the correct English page but now we are waiting for the Serbian page to appear. If it is my mistake, please tell me, we made a double-check yesterday to make sure that we've got the right page. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, please look at the document about a meeting of the Supreme Command. The meeting took place on the 21st of January, 1993. General, sir, here Radovan Karadzic speaks about the axis to the Drina. It says the situation is tragic because they control 60 kilometres of the Drina bank. If you remember the events, could you please tell us what part of the Drina bank is Radovan Karadzic talking about?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when I'm supposed to start talking. I don't have the transcript on the left-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher be of assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. First of all, I have some doubts about the date, 21 January 1993, because the 21st January 1993, Karadzic and Mladic were either in Geneva or in London; in any case, they were abroad, which means that no session of the Supreme Command could have taken place on that date. Second of all, on the 21st of January, Vance Owen's plan was violated in Ravni Kotari when Croatia attacked the area of the Serbian Krajina. I don't have anything against that session or the contents of the words that Karadzic used but the date is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But could you please answer my question: What part of the river bank did Karadzic have in mind and what event did he have in mind when he uttered those words?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Karadzic is referring to the central part of the Drina around Visegrad because on that date Visegrad power plant was attacked by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the attack on Skelani and Bajina Basta? Did it happen in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Skelani was attacked on the 16th of January and the attack lasted until the 23rd of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The attack that we are talking about, the attack on Skelani, and you say that it took place on the 16th, what happened? Were Serb villages attacked, plundered and torched around Bajina Basta and its environs, as much as you remember?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the fire was open on the territory of Serbia. I know that during the war two shells were fired on Mali Zvornik, I don't know if that was a mistake or not. And as for Skelani, about 20 Serbian villages and hamlets were attacked before the Muslims reached Skelani. And those villages were completely destroyed and the population was expelled across the bridge near Bajina Basta. About 20.000 people fled. The unit that defended Skelani which was an independent Skelani unit broke up. They were crushed. We could not deal with the problem with our units from Podrinje. I spoke to the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps and ordered him to send me reinforcement. He sent two battalions, and as soon as those battalions arrived within 24 hours the situation was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is stated here, or rather, Karadzic says we had to take decisive action. What does he mean when he says that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what he means. I'm sure that I did not attend that session. I'm looking at the list of the participants and what people said. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page, please. Page 78 in B/C/S, page 80 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, look at Karadzic's words at the bottom of the page, both in Serbian and in English. Karadzic says somebody decided that Skelani should be evacuated. Do you know who decided that and why?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what information Karadzic had about the evacuation of Skelani. That was not done according to any plan. The population simply fled. I know when that was happening, that was happening on the 17 and the 18th of January. I sent my deputy, Colonel Ilic, to try and stop the population and the Skelani battalion. The colonel came to the bridge. He opened fire into the air but to no avail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic asked you, on the basis of this text, whether you could tell us who decided to evacuate Skelani. If you know, tell us. If you say, I don't know who decided, or even if you say, No one decided, please tell us, but don't give us the whole story of Skelani because you are not asked to bring that story. Do you know who decided to evacuate Skelani two or three days before this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no decision to that effect. People simply fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And can we now look at the following page in the same document, B/C/S 79, English 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is about a meeting which took place in President Cosic's office. According to the document, the date is the same, 21st January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we go to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The following page, General Panic - at the very bottom of the page - at the meeting with President Cosic, he says that the situation on the Drina River is very bad. My question to you, sir, is this: Why was the situation on the Drina River considered at the highest level in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and President Cosic's office? Why was that situation so important to merit a discussion at such a high level?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on that day preparation started for the peace conference in Geneva. The leaders of Republika Srpska, Karadzic and Mladic and some other people, were also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the situation and the flight of some 20.000 people, threat to the facilities along the border, do you agree that this had a rather unfavourable effect on the security situation in the Republic of Serbia, i.e., the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 65 ter 5605. B/C/S page 336 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, before we continue, all three judges are lost as far as the relevance of the line of this questioning is -- the questioning is. If you could assist, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can do that. The events along the Drina River about which the General has testified caused an operation by the government of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the engagement of the military and the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. The accused in this case participated in that operation to a certain extent which is why we would like to explain the circumstances that led to the operation at that -- a number of Prosecution witnesses mentioned in their testimonies as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are just talking about the background what caused some operational activity and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is there dispute about what triggered, whether there was concern about the situation at the Drina River, for example, something we listened to in the last one or two minutes and why it should be discussed at a high level? Is there any dispute about such a worrying situation at the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We haven't address this particular issue, but with respect to the issue in Skelani and along the Drina, that's -- we have already agreed that there were attacks against Serbs there. There were infiltrations. That's all a matter of agreement in the course of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Petrovic, why do we go through it again? Let's focus on the matters which are really in dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, please look at this entry of 23rd September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, these are demands of the VRS from the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a conversation between General Mladic and General Perisic. And, yes, you are right, General Mladic is asking for something but verbally, not in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Look at item 12 where it says "Issues of status of officers." Could you explain briefly, if you know, what was General Mladic asking from the Army of Yugoslavia regarding the status of officers?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the Army of Yugoslavia, that is to say, the leadership of Yugoslavia, took upon themselves the obligation to pay and provide housing and other benefits to the officers of the Army of Yugoslavia who either remained or went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those are issues of their status. We did receive reserve officers but we could not pay them according to their rank. Those issues were dealt with by the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday seven and a half thousand officers and NCOs that served in the VRS but were paid funded by the Army of Yugoslavia, did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that it was an agreement with the Army of Yugoslavia that was signed by Vice-President Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Concerning those seven and a half thousand officers, what was provided except their salaries?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their next salaries were paid, benefits, health and pension insurance were paid directly to their accounts in Belgrade, housing was provided to VRS personnel, just as to the personnel of the Army of Yugoslavia, and medical insurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many officers in total served in the Army of Republika Srpska, roughly, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many officers? I can't tell you the figure but I can tell you that 21 per cent of professional officers and 79 per cent of reserve officers served in the VRS. The 21 per cent were paid by VJ, the 79 per cent by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood correctly, all professional officers were paid by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the counsel not overlap and give us a pause between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited not to overlap, Mr. Petrovic. So could you please repeat your last question, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, members of the Main Staff of the VRS, corps commanders, brigade commanders, commanders of lower tactical units, all those officers were financed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right because we had commanders from battalion level to brigade level, and those are the 79 reserve -- 79 per cent reserve officers. The VJ paid only professional officers who made up 21 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's make things simpler in this way. The highest-ranking officers in the VRS and the most responsible officers in the VRS were paid by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, could we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would agree the most easily if we say the VJ paid officers, graduates of military academies and graduates of middle military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's clear then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is there dispute about the payment of the high-ranking officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was actually contemplating and standing up and objecting to relevance. I am not sure what the relevance is of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, there's no dispute about it. Relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the relevance lies in the measure of contribution to the joint criminal enterprise charged against my client. I can elaborate on that, if necessary, but that is the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there's no dispute about high-ranking officers being paid not by the VRS but by the JNA or what used to be the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be unable to verify precise percentages, but in general principle there's no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why are you spending so much time on one simple question? Is it true, Mr. Milovanovic - you can do that even without that - a large number of high-ranking officers were paid by the VJ rather than by the VRS? The answer will be yes and we move on to the next one. Why -- please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Item 13 in this document we are looking at, the status of repair shops. Orao and Kosmos what is this about? Why is Mladic discussing this with Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The repair shops Orao or Kosmos were for military equipment; Orao for aircraft, and Kosmos was a universal factory for the repair and maintenance of some rocket systems for defence. There was a problem at the outset of the war: Who was going to manage those companies, the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska or the Main Staff? And I know it was decided that all repair shops in the territory of Republika Srpska and special-purpose industries, that is, those producing ammunition, should be managed by the Main Staff and that's how it was done until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at another point in the same document. Page 338 in the manuscript or in the copy and English page 330. Bottom of the page, please, where General Novakovic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what is VOJIN, just in one sentence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Air observation notification and guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This VOJIN system in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska, was it integrated with the same system in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All VOJIN systems were integrated within friendly countries in one region; that is to say, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Republika Srpska, and the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 387 in the copy and 389 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I request that Mr. Petrovic read out the dates of these entries, it would be much easier for us to follow where he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please follow this suggestion, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour. I will now tell you the date. 19 October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May I put my question, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General Perisic is saying that military conscripts and officers, if I understand correctly, should be directed -- he says those who don't want to serve in the RS and RSK should be expelled from the army. Should be expelled full stop. Do you know that troops who did not want to serve from -- serve in the RS and the RSK were indeed expelled from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this was started just as Perisic became Chief of the General Staff and he was very diligent about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting of the 21st October, 1993, page 389 in the copy, and in English it's 390.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, look at this meeting, please. You can see the beginning on this page before us and then we should turn the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, the verification of promotions into general, you said something about it, but clarify it. Who promotes and who confirms the promotion? Can people be promoted without being confirmed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no confirmation without promotion. Its the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska that promotes officers into generals and it is verified by the Supreme Command; that is to say, the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From what moment on does a prospective general of the VRS become a general, really?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain this using my own example. I was promoted into lieutenant-general by decree of the president of Republika Srpska on the 28th of June, 1994, and my rank was verified sometime on the 25th December, 1995. I received a salary in the meantime of a lieutenant -- of a colonel, not lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Of major-general, not lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 391 in the copy and 393 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You attended this meeting too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It says the discussion goes on at the session. Officers are requested from the FRY for the Gatac Brigade. What we see here, was it normal practice to request the return or the sending of officers from some VJ units? It says lieutenant-colonels and colonels; one in Topola, one in Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the practice. When the initial agreements were made for officers who were natives of Republika Srpska to come back, it was agreed then that officers serving in Kosovo do not have to come to Republika Srpska. It will be recorded as service in the war and similarly exempted where officers serving in some units that couldn't be spared. But as for Colonel Andzic, he was a native of Herzegovina and they needed him to become commander of this Gatac Brigade and this Milivoj Radovic was also requested. This Gatac Brigade used to be a TO brigade and then it was renamed into an infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. At the same meeting, on page 394 in B/C/S and 396 in the English translation, there is a reference to the activities that needed to be carried out, the shortening of the front line as a way to fight Dudakovic's forces, and to assist Fikret Abdic. My question is this: How is Fikret Abdic assisted by the shortening of the front line?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's clarify one thing. I had the text in front of me a minute ago but I don't see it anymore because it's too small. The 2nd Corps should fight Drekovic's force, not Dudakovic's forces. Drekovic was commander before Fikret Abdic. Konjic is mentioned here. Drekovic was moved from Bihac and became the commander of the Muslim Herzegovina Corps. I believe it was the 6th Corps. Drekovic was here and there at the same time. However, in the first came [as interpreted] when our 2nd Corps is mentioned, the person made a mistake and used Drekovic's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So my question is: How is Abdic assisted by the shortening of the front line facing the corps in Cazina Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shortening of the front line is a tactical operation. By shortening the front line, you don't lose much territory but you liberate some of your forces that you can use to assist Fikret Abdic. I already spoke at great length about what was the army of Fikret Abdic, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was this task ever implemented as it is stated here? I remind you that that was in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the operation was implemented. I know that Karadzic signed an agreement with Fikret Abdic but that was just the beginning of Fikret Abdic's career and I really can't say much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 5606. In B/C/S it's page 53 and the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is the front page describing the meeting which took place on the 13th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you obviously attended that meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say here that you wanted assistance on the right bank of the Drina. Do you remember why you requested that? And that request was addressed at the representatives of the FRY who were also participants in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to seek assistance from the FRY in the central and upper Drina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A few lines down, Karadzic says General Milovanovic has talked about slow moving things or side things. Why did he say that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say side things but slow moving things; i.e., things that should follow in the future, at least that's what it says here. I don't know what he said exactly but I know that he didn't agree with my words, and this is why: He wanted to carry out an offensive around Sarajevo before some peace talks that were supposed to start on the 21st and the 22nd in Geneva. He made use of Mladic's absence from the front line and he consulted with me, and then he said that we should take Zuc, Mojmilo and Sarajevo, as well as some features and facilities in the town itself, that there should be encirclement around Sarajevo to liberate the Praca valley that UNPROFOR had given to Muslims as a corridor between Sarajevo and Gorazde. In that conversation which took place on the 10th of December, I refused his proposals and I tried to convince him that that was impossible, that our military was not prepared to do that, and then he called me back again on the 12th on the eve of the meeting, that is described here, he invited me to come to Pale. Again, he tried to persuade me to ask assistance from the FRY, the assistance in life force. Again, I refused his proposals, and that's how I left for the meeting because Mladic and I could not both be absent from the front line, that's why I went to the meeting. In the first part of my discussion I uttered a sentence and I said that if we wanted to comply with Karadzic's request, we had to rely only on our forces, that we should not drag the FRY into war. In my second discussion, I wanted help on the right bank of the Drina, if FRY was, indeed, willing to be engaged, and I requested whatever is stated here. I knew that in Leskovac and Vranje there were two battalion -- tank battalions and I requested those tanks. Karadzic didn't like that and that's why he said what he did, that I'm talking about slow moving things or Weinguard [as interpreted] things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 57 in B/C/S and 58 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the middle of that page, it says: Badza. The forces that are request are indeed need and I support that. My only question to you is this: Who is Badza?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badza was the general lieutenant in the police or lieutenant-general in the police. He was killed in Belgrade. I really can't remember his name. I believe that his family name was Stojicic. I believe that he was responsible for the Special Police Units in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, are you really serious in asking this witness who Badza is? We've heard about Badza for a year now on a daily basis. Do we need this witness to tell us who Badza is? Or is there any dispute about this Badza being present at this meeting, then ask the witness whether he knows whether the Badza mentioned here was present at that meeting and who he is so that we -- and identify him. But to say we see the name Badza, could you tell us what the name Badza, who you considered him to be, is that really after a year that -- but please explain yourself, don't take too much time for it because you have only 10 minutes left. Is it that this witness knows something about the presence of this person and if --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to see what this witness knows about that person because I wanted to know what the perception of Badza was in the eyes of this witness. I didn't put the question to him because I thought that nobody here knows who Badza is but I wanted to hear from a general in the Serbian army whether he knew who that person was. I thought it was important but if Trial Chamber thinks that this is not relevant at this point in time, I will not dwell upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. But then ask a different question than "Do you know who Badza is," because then we get the answer and no additional information whatsoever, mainly that he thinks that he remembers the family name which sounds rather familiar to us, unless there's any dispute about this Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could assist Mr. Petrovic, General Milovanovic spoke about a meeting or an encounter he had with Badza in his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now we know that what Mr. Milovanovic told us on the very general question, the very general question being ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I have just a few more questions and that will be my cross-examination to an end. I will not dwell upon this issue any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we now look at page 42 in the same document, that's in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held on the 22nd of November, 1993. General, sir, you attended the meeting, if I am not mistaken, and you took the floor. You spoke about the need to launch war production. You talked about materiel and technical equipment, and the overhaul of the equipment. First of all, tell us why is this mentioned at the meeting? You were the one who spoke about that so I suppose that you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not sure that I was present at the meeting on the 22nd of November, 1993. However, here when General Mladic is quoted, he is quoted as saying General Milovanovic has just informed us about this or that or the other. It's possible that a day before on my birthday I informed Mladic about that. I was not at that meeting in Belgrade and you can see that Djukic and Mladic from the Main Staff attended, the assistant commander for logistics and the commander himself. I wasn't at that meeting. I told you yesterday that I was responsible for the distribution of a strategic materiel, and here I just suggested what the commander of the Main Staff should do and how he should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us, please, materiel and technical equipment, were they repaired in the FRY and what materiel and equipment was repaired?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were they repaired in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the Army of Republika Srpska inherited almost all the giants in terms of repairs facilities of the former JNA, save for the company in Cacak which is in Serbia. We had Hadzici for the repairs of heavy artillery. We also had Kosmos for the repairs of rockets. We also had a facility called Orao to repair airplane engines, and we, ourselves, repaired the materiel and equipment belonging to the Army of Yugoslavia. They paid us for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at just one more document which is 5607, pages 34 and 35, but let's first look at 34 in B/C/S and 33 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It says here "Co-ordination." This is about a meeting which took place on the 19th of January, 1994. What kind of a meeting was that? That meeting bears the name co-ordination. What type of a meeting was that, why is it called co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Because it would be General Djukic, the assistant commander for logistics, that chaired this meeting, but when I look at the contents, I can see that they are talking about recruits and about the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following page, maybe that will help you shed some light on who co-ordinated whom, what, and why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two minutes left, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know, never mind, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that it was the co-ordination of logistics between the Army of Republika Srpska, the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Fikret Abdic's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I have no more questions nor witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Groome, are you ready to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you will now be further examined by Mr. Groome who, as you know, is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milovanovic. I do not have many questions for you today. I do want to clarify some of the evidence you provide in response to questions by Mr. Jordash and Mr. Petrovic this week. My first question relates to a date. I will read a portion of Tuesday's transcript, and I ask you to focus on the date and tell us whether the transcript has correctly he recorded your evidence about this date. At transcript page 15348, Mr. Jordash asked you the following question: "Now, I appreciate from what you've told us before that you were not with him during the events in Srebrenica in 1995, during the massacres there; is that correct?" The pronoun "him" was a reference to General Mladic. Your response was, and it begins at line 14: "Beginning with the 28th of October, 1994, until the 15th of October, 1994, I was not with Mladic all the time. I was in the west in Drvar and Banja Luka ..." And it continues on. Has the transcript correctly recorded your evidence with respect to the transcript that you were in the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it seems somewhat illogical that you were somewhere from the 28th of October in the year 1994 until the 15th of October in the year 1994?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it was 1995. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the transcript should read that you were there until the 15th of October 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at transcript page 15338 and following, on Tuesday, Mr. Jordash asked you a number of questions regarding the military airfields used by the VRS during the conflict. I would like to now ask you some questions to clarify your evidence. As I understood your evidence, you were referring to military air facilities under the control of the VRS and not every air strip in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the airfields used by the VRS. And speaking of airfields, I meant to ask for a correction. When I was looking on the map, on the non-existent part of the map, an airfield near Glamoc, I marked Crni-Lug 2 or 3 centimetres to the north, whereas it is actually to the south of Crni-Lug village. I later looked and map, so it's not to the north of Crni-Lug that Glamoc Polje airfield, it's to the south of Crni-Lug.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash may have another opportunity to ask you questions and may seek to clarify the precise location. Were there other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina where small aircraft or helicopters could land, apart from the airfields that you identified?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Helicopters were able to land anywhere. We had heliports in Crni Rijeka, near Han Pijesak, for the Main Staff, a heliport at Pale for the Supreme Command, another heliport in Kalinovik, in all major free places near barracks. As for auxiliary airfields where aircraft could take off and land, apart from these four, I don't know about any others and because we didn't use them and there was no need for me to be interested in them. It was Bratunac, Zaluzani, Mahovljani, Bijeljina and the one in Glamoc Polje. Sorry, not in Bijeljina but Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, if a helicopter was needed in an military operation, is it possible to create an improvised landing area for that helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was only up to the pilot to choose a flat piece of land, not to overturn the helicopter, and at night-time you do it by crossing the headlights of four vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do I correctly understand your evidence that to create an improvised airfield at night, you simply need to arrange four vehicles with their headlights on and the intersection of the headlights indicates the place where the helicopter should land?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he will, in fact, be able to see where he is landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in 1997 Frenki Simatovic, one of the accused in this case, gave a speech recounting the history of the Red Beret unit in a ceremony attended by senior officials of Serbia. A transcript of that narrative is in evidence as P61. Mr. Simatovic said that the Red Berets acquired helicopters in May of 1991 and landed those helicopters on a number of improvised airfields in Bosnia. Are you able to say whether or not this occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I object to that. I think that the speech aspects of what Mr. Simatovic actually said should be put to the witness. Mr. Groome has actually, I think, mis-characterised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If there is any I dispute about what was said [overlapping speakers] ... please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will quote, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to read you the quote from that portion of the speech: "In May 1991, an air helicopter squadron was formed which transported tonnes of special shipments, equipment, troops, and machinery from the improvised airfields of Medin Polje, Petrovac, Velika Popina, Srb and Udbina and carried out numerous complex tasks while war operations were ongoing." Again, my question to you is: Are you able to say from your own knowledge whether what Mr. Simatovic says about improvised airfields is true or is not true?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in Macedonia at the time. There was no war at the time. It was 1991. The SFRY was at its full strength. Wherever helicopters flew, it was legal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the -- the question has been answered by the first four words, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, we need a full transcript, unfortunately, so we'll have to ask the witness to repeat what he said, although the answer is clear already. Could you please repeat the last part after you said: "The SFRY was at its full strength. Wherever helicopters flew, it was legal." And what did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, I said I know that Medin Polje World War II used to be a partisan airfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, Mr. Simatovic goes further in the speech to say that the Red Berets' use of aircraft remained undetected by NATO. Are you able to tell us how a helicopter might be used in a way that evaded detection by a sophisticated military organisation such as NATO? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I also flew by helicopter and I was never detected until General Morillon complained about it. It's called a swiping type of flying where the helicopter flies according to the lay of the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could I ask that P2933 be brought to our screen. It is a one-page entry from General Mladic's notebook. It is dated 16th of December, 1991. And this is J000-3714.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, yesterday at transcript page 15436, Mr. Jordash put to you that there was no mention of Stanisic prior to the 2nd of July, 1993. I would like to show you an entry in the diary related to when references can be found to the State Security of Serbia. General, I ask you to look at the entry that's now on the screen before you, again from the 16th of December, 1991. In it we see Mladic recording information provided by a person he refers to as Rade Siptar and records his -- that's information as: "Dule Orlovic, Filipovic - Fica and Frenki," and after Frenki's name in parentheses is the word "Serbian DB." "They want to give some 3.000 barrels to the Muslims in Bihac." Now, my first question to you regarding this entry, General, is: Based on your experience with General Mladic, when he wrote "3.000 barrels," what was that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army when you say barrel, it means infantry weapons, it could be a pistol, rifle, anything up to the 12.7 millimetres machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct that the B/C/S word that Mladic used was "cevi," c-e-v-i? Is that the word that is used in the original of the diary?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. That's what is written, "3.000 cevi," and I'm making my comment as an expert that it is -- that it means infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know where further questions by my learned friend are going, but I'm concerned because I don't know from which part of my examination or Mr. Jordash's examination these questions follow concerning this part of the report. If my learned friend is now leading new evidence, I don't think it's right -- it's the right time and that should have been done a year ago, not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, or as I prefaced my question, on Tuesday at transcript 15436, I am sorry, it was yesterday, Mr. Jordash put to the witness that there was no mention of Mr. Stanisic in his diary until the 23rd of July, 1993. This is a clear reference to the Serbian State Security Service much earlier than that date and predates the commencement of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a reference to Frenki of the Serbian state security. It's not a reference to Stanisic. And they are not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, the word "barrel" in English can mean the barrel of a gun, it can also mean a container to contain oil or some other liquid. Is there any interpretation of the word "cevi" as used in this sentence that can mean something other than the barrel of a gun or an infantry weapon?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian language is not very clear. It could be a tube, a pipe, like a drain pipe or a smoke pipe or something in the middle of a sheet, but Mladic wouldn't be talking about sewage or water-supply pipes, something as -- as something in which the DB of Serbia would be involved. It's barrels of a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, this is three and a half months before the outbreak of the conflict in Bosnia, and Bihac is in Bosnia. Any idea why Frenki would want to give 3.000 infantry weapons to the Muslims of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that Frenki is providing "cevi" barrels. I can understand it in two ways. Perhaps Frenki is providing barrels or maybe Frenki discovered that somebody else is providing barrels. I believe it's the seconds because political parties had started to arm the citizens, the SDS is arming Serbs and the SDA is arming Muslims. I cannot really be sure whether Frenki is providing guns or he discovered somebody else was providing guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient place to take the morning break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a convenient moment. We'll take a break and we resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Just one correction from the interpreters. At page 24, line 21, the proper translation of the type of flying is low flying or hedge hopping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was just wondering whether following the scape of the land, whether that would be at low altitude. We resume at quarter to 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, I'd like to move to a different topic now. On Tuesday Mr. Jordash asked you about establishing effective communication with subordinate units of the VRS and you said at transcript page 15342: "I was told to organise communications with our subordinated units that we had at the time and to start receiving reports from the field effectively on the 12th of May." Do I take from this that beginning on the 12th of May, 1992, you began the process of building effective communications between the VRS Main Staff and the military structures subordinate to it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did it take before you established what you believed to be effective communication with subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I established the communications in the course of the 12th because I had inherited the war time command posts of the former JNA corps so I didn't have many technical issues to solve.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the VRS, like other military organisations, had several levels from the Main Staff down to the commander of a company or tank unit. When you said that you were able to establish effective communications on the 12th, is it your evidence that you were able to establish such communications between the Main Staff and all subordinate VRS units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only between the Main Staff corps commands and the command of the air force and air defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it take longer to establish effective communication with all the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That took around a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you use the word "communication," do you mean to include both reports coming into the Main Staff and directives or orders going out to the Main Staff to subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several types of communications, radio communications, wire communications, signals communications and courier communications. Radio and wire communications were set up in the course of that day so we were able, both verbally and in writing, to communicate with corps commands using teletype.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long before you had the full plethora of communications up and running?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the first two type of communications, radio and wire, that was done on the 12th, and the rest gradually. I can't tell you exactly how long it takes to provide courier communications. Depends on the distance between the correspondence. From the Main Staff to the Drina Corps it took two hours, from the Main Staff to the 1st Krajina Corps six hours, to another corps 12 hours, depending on how long the courier takes to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, also in answer to Mr. Jordash's questions, you spoke about the daily briefing, and you said: "Every morning between 6.00 and 7.00, the Main Staff received reports from subordinates. It would be either General Mladic or myself who received them." I will ask you in a few minutes about one of these particular briefings but can I ask that you tell us now how it was decided whether you would receive the briefing or whether Mladic would receive that briefing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports were supposed to be received by General Mladic. In his absence, I would receive them as his deputy. I told you we shared an office and it was not hard to see whether he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if he was absent, would you take any steps to brief him about what was the information you received at the morning briefing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the obligation to call him. He had the obligation to call me and inquire if there was anything new.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it his practice do so?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know approximately what time of the morning or the day he would call to receive a briefing or an update about the morning briefing of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on his location. If he was on the front line, that would usually be in the morning and he would call me from one of the corps commands. If he was outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, he would usually call in the evening when all the conditions for communicating with me were there, especially if he was outside of Serbia even.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to address a number of exhibits that Mr. Jordash worked with over the course of the last two days. Yesterday at transcript page T15409 Mr. Jordash showed you 65 ter 5602, pages 40 and 51, corresponding to ERN numbers J000-1170 and J000-1181 of the original notebook. Both of these entries are from a meeting on the 15th of September, 1992. I want to return to page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I could ask that 65 ter 5602, e-court page 40 in the English be brought to our screens. I believe it's also page 40 in the B/C/S. And it's J000-1170.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Jordash showed you this yesterday, he referred you to a portion where the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps is talking about Mauzer. And I'll wait till we have that on the screen. Can you see it now on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jordash didn't work with the continuation of the report, particularly with respect to Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we turn to the next page in both of these versions, the translation and the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like you to read what the commander continued to say with respect to point number 2, Ljubisa Savic. He says: "The morale of our unit has been weakened from the moment of engagement of the MUP of Serbia." My question to you is based on your experience and work with General Mladic, can you help us to understand what is meant by this entry?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he meant. I don't know where the MUP of Serbia was engaged and why. Yesterday Mr. Jordash only asked me whether on the previous page a reference to Ljubisa Savic was also a reference to Mauzer to which I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would the fact that General Mladic wrote this comment under the heading, point 2, "Ljubisa Savic," indicate whether he believed Mauzer or Ljubisa Savic had some relationship to the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only answer that by saying probably, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to e-court page 55 in English and the same page in the original, and the J number is J000-1185.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A bit later in the same entry on the page I believe you now see before you, Branko Grujic, president of the Zvornik municipality, speaks. He says: "Under the command of Marko Pavlovic we did everything." A few lines later he speaks about someone named Dzokanovic. And that's D-z-o-k-a-n-o-v-i-c. And he says, "Dzokanovic is causing lots of problems around Zvornik." You've given evidence about Zvornik over the last couple of days. Are you familiar with this person Dzokanovic and who he might be.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't have the handwritten B/C/S version which exists in English. Now I have it. I don't know who that Dzokanovic or Dukanovic was, and I also don't know who Marko Pavlovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit. Can I ask now that P2543, another entry from Mladic's notebook, be brought to the screen. It's date the November 22nd 1995. It appears to be a record of a briefing meeting. Could I ask that General Milovanovic be shown the first page so that he can orient himself to the date and the meeting. The ERN of this page is J000-0195.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, if you let us know when you have finished reading that page, I've few questions before I take you to a specific portion.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does it start with General Tomic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The translators or the people who have transcribed it recorded that as General Talic. Could it be General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, you are right. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you've read it if you indicate that and I'll ask you a question before I turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, just above the name of General Talic is the text "briefing by the officers." Would this indicate that this entry is a record of the Main Staff briefing of the 22nd of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not at the Main Staff but at the forward command post of the Main Staff which means that the briefing took place in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is this the same daily meeting that you've referred to earlier in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was something else but only the commanders of the Krajina units were involved, the first and the 2nd Krajina Corps, the training centre, the anti-aircraft defence and the air force. All those commands were based in Banja Luka at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we advance to e-court page 4 in the original in English and the ERN is J000-0918.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the intervening pages after the notes under Talic's name we can see similar brief notes under the names of General Tomanic, General Ninkovic, General Gvero, Colonel Djurdjevic, Colonel Kukobat, and then your name, General Milovanovic, appears. Are we correct to conclude that the text appearing under each name is the information that that particular officer provided on that day?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see my own name. The last name I see is General Ninkovic. I am sorry, yes, General Milovanovic. I can see that. General Mladic actually recorded what we said to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you to read what he recorded you as having said that day, and it goes on to the next page, so when you've read this page, please indicate that and I'll ask that we advance to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just inquire as to how this arises during re-examination? Or from the cross-examination, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we ask perhaps the witness to take off the earphones, I think is best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovanovic, I don't know whether I ever asked you, so you speak -- do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you take off your earphones. I might have asked it before, but -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday, I think it was the day before, Mr. Jordash spent a considerable amount of time eliciting that there was an order in June of 1992 prohibiting paramilitaries from being present on the territory under the control of the VRS. And if you look in this particular entry, the entry that he is reading now and that I will ask him about refers to a delegation of members of State Security Service and the word paramilitary is even used to describe them. So I'm using this to counter Mr. Jordash's suggestion that the order of June 1992 prevented or did not permit members of the -- of Arkan's unit, of Bozovic and others to be on the territory of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the first thing is that the word "paramilitary" is not used to describe them. I don't accept this arises during -- from the cross-examination, but I withdraw the objection because I think Mr. Groome having made that assertion, Mr. Milovanovic might be able to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then could you please put on your earphones again, Mr. Milovanovic. You may proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps while we were speaking, you have already completed reading the notes under your name. Have you done that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read the page that is in front of me. I don't know whether there is anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is some. It continues on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if we could please advance to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Indicate when you have completed reading the entry and then I'll ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to our conversation or our discussion out of the hearing of the witness, it is the first line of this page that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read the page. It was quite easy to read the first half of the page. The bottom part, however, is somewhat less legible, so I'm not sure whether my understanding of it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an important matter, and I have a printed copy. If there's no objection, could we provide the witness with a printed copy of this and perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections, so please proceed as suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, there's now a printed copy of that exhibit before you. Perhaps you can advise us whether that's more legible than the television screen?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a printed copy. This is again handwriting, a handwritten copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I misunderstood you. So you would prefer to have what, a typed, what a transcriber read from it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That will take a few moments for us to locate. Perhaps I can ask you some questions and if you are -- you may be able to answer them with the portion that you are able to read, and if you think you would like to read the other one, still, at the end of my question, we'll do our best to get that as quickly as possible. Now, my first question relates to the information that you provide General Mladic that a team from the State Security of Serbia appeared here. When you said they appeared here, did you mean that they appeared at the forward command post in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two before that President Karadzic, who was in Banja Luka as well to discuss the defence of Banja Luka, told me that some people would arrive from the MUP of Serbia. He didn't say DB. He told me that I should receive those units that would arrive from Serbia. Those would be the Special Police Units that would help us to defend Banja Luka. I know only too well that that Filipovic arrived as well as the colonel whom I met near Kladusa. He was in the company of Mr. Frenki. His name was Bozovic and he spoke with a Montenegrin accent. They told me that they would arrive and they mentioned different figures. First they mentioned three brigades and then the number was reduced down to some 900 men. And they were looking for a place where they would be billeted. Since they were police officers, I thought that that was part of co-operation between the two MUPs, the MUP of Republika Srpska and the MUP of Serbia. That's why I suggested that they should contact our MUP. The MUP had some premises near Banja Luka. The name of that facility was Rakovacke Bare. My suggestion was that they should be billeted there. I don't know anything else about those police officers. I don't think that they ever arrived, but as it says here, Arkan appeared on the front line with 300 Tigers. He was chased away in 1992 and then he returned in 1995. I discovered his presence when I learned that he had beaten up some Serbian officers. I asked for Karadzic for a meeting to ask him who had approved Arkan's arrival because I was firm in claiming that Arkan had entered my area of responsibility without my approval. Karadzic finally after my ultimatum organised a meeting with Arkan in Banja Luka in the temporary office of the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all I can tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's a few very precise questions I'd like to ask you about this entry. Do you know how they came, whether this delegation from the State Security Service of Serbia came by road or by helicopter or some other means of transportation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never bothered to ask them. They appeared in my office in the command of the 1st Corps. I used at the office of the chief of the corps staff, General Lekovic. Our military police escorted them to the building and since I knew that people from the MUP of Serbia were supposed to arrive, I received them and I talked to them about the topic that I just covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Filipovic was there and perhaps Bozovic was there as well, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps if we work through my questions one at a time, we'll be able to understand your evidence a bit more clearly. In this entry, you not only talk about the visit of this delegation but you also, as you've just told us, you refer to the arrival of 300 of Arkan's volunteers. My question to you is simply: Does the fact that both of these --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to jump up. Could Mr. Groome be careful about leading on these issues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does the -- does the fact that both of these entries are in the same -- both of these -- both of this information, or all of this information, is in the same entry indicate anything about the time relationship between those two events?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please explain?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First the two police colonels arrived, Filipovic and Bozovic. Arkan did not arrive at that time. He simply appeared somewhere in the vicinity of Kljuc and Prijedor. But that happened a few days later, or perhaps even a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I correct in understanding from what you've just told us that you reported the information about Bozovic and Filipovic approximately a month after it occurred?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I reported the information about Rakovacke Bare to those men immediately because they left and I never saw them again after that. And as for Arkan, as I've already told you, he appeared somewhat later. Perhaps even a months later he appeared on the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then can you explain to us how that would appear in this particular entry, this entry of the 22nd of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, the text reads "300 Arkan's volunteers arrived and were put into the RS MUP," which suggests that when this was written that they had arrived already and that they were already put into the RS MUP. That's what Mr. Groome's question is focusing upon, Mr. Groome, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was on the day when the briefing took place and I suppose that I related to Mladic the history of the events. I'm not saying that they appeared on the day when the briefing took place. They had appeared earlier than that and the briefing took place on the 22nd of September. I can't remember when exactly they appeared, but, in any case, they appeared before the briefing and Arkan also appeared before the briefing and I can claim that in view of the fact that I was in a position to brief the commander about the strength of his unit. Arkan appeared on the 16th of September or a day or two later. I know that because on the 16th of September we lost Kljuc. Kljuc fell into Muslim hands and the first place where Arkan appeared was around Kljuc, somewhere near Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, how did you know that Bozovic and the others that represented themselves to be members of the State Security Service of Serbia, how did you know that they were, in fact, who they were representing themselves to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may be mistaken but I believe that they introduced themselves -- according to the witness, the witness said that they had introduced themselves as representatives of the MUP of Serbia. That's the way I understood the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time we see in the document a team from the Serbian DB state security appeared. So we have two versions of the way in which they introduced themselves, one written and one as just explained per the witness. I think everyone keeps that in its mind. What seems to be the gist of the question put to the witness is that how would he know that they were who they claimed they were, isn't it, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I can be a little more precise in my question, if I can take another try at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've given us evidence that Mr. Karadzic had foretold of the arrival of some people from the Serbian MUP. Now, can I take it that by the time these men arrived at your office they would have had to have gone through some security --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we -- objection to the leading nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Mr. Groome, you wanted to ask the witness whether they had to go through any kind of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, prior to arriving in your office, would this delegation have had to have identified themselves to gain access to the compound where you were, the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policeman from the centre post called me to tell me that people from the MUP of Serbia had arrived. And since Karadzic had told me only a few days before that that they would arrive, I received them. It was not up to me to take their IDs. They introduced themselves as Filipovic and Bozovic. I knew that they were supposed to arrive, and they immediately started discussing the issue of billeting, those men, that they were supposed to follow them. I did not check their identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know how you learned and in turn conveyed to General Mladic that they were from the state security of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know how I conveyed that to General Mladic. However, those men spoke about Special Police Units. I knew intuitively that they were talking about the DB of Serbia. I really don't know why it occurred to me to tie them to the state security, but I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jordash asked you a series of questions with respect to the decision by the VRS Main Staff to expel paramilitaries in June of 1992. Were members of the Serbian MUP who were present in Bosnia engaged in official work considered paramilitaries for the purpose of that decision of June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Serbian MUP was not engaged in that. As I told you yesterday, the commander had talked to the commanders of those militaries. The process lasted from the 12th of May to the 28th of June. Then it was finalised by General Mladic's order on chasing the paramilitaries away from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what I'm asking you now is: Did that order include members of the Serbian MUP who were present in Bosnia-Herzegovina on official business?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were military organisations that were not part of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my next question is: How would members of the VRS be able to distinguish between people that came from Serbia who were Serbian MUP officials on official business, and paramilitaries that had come from Serbia and were to be expelled?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, those who arrived on official business from Serbia did not have to hide. Their ID was checked at border crossings. Their arrival was announced. And as for the others, and I told you what paramilitary units those were which were not within the system of the VRS, they were Mauzer's Panthers, Arkan's Tigers, Zuca and Crni, and several groups around Sarajevo. We knew very well who paramilitaries were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you use the word "their IDs were checked," are you speaking about a national identification card or a Serbian MUP identification card?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it was only on the 27th of July, 1992 that we agreed how border crossings would be controlled with the MUP of Serbia. Until then it was the police of Republika Srpska that controlled border crossings. As Chief of Staff, I was not duty-bound which of the politicians entered the territory of Republika Srpska. It was the police of Republika Srpska who had to control that. It was only after the 27th of July that we and the then minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, and the deputy prime minister, Milan Trbojevic, agreed that at some border crossings there would be mixed patrol, military and civilian police patrols, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If someone had a Serbian MUP identification cart on their person, did that permit them to move freely in the area controlled by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody was able to move in the combat zone, and the person coming was certainly not coming to inspect the army. He was coming for negotiations with MUP or politicians, not the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now see P2544. This is an entry a week later from the 29th of September, 1995, and records a meeting between Mladic and Karadzic. It is a single page that's been put on e-court and it bears the number J000-0938.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, in this relatively brief entry there is a reference to Jovica Stanisic which says: "Jovica Stanisic is angry about something. (He gave 300 of his men and the US is begrudging us for having advertised Arkan)." As I said, this occurs one week after your briefing to General Mladic that Arkan had arrived in the area. Can you help us understand this entry?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, the 300 that is recorded here, he gave 300 of his men, is this a reference to the Serbian MUP personnel that was discussed a week earlier with you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't know whether these policemen, promised me by Filipovic and Bozovic, came at all, but I said that Arkan arrived with 300 of his men and I don't know who organised it. I don't know that to this day, and I don't mind telling you that I look forward to testifying in Karadzic so I can have it out with him. I still don't know who approved Arkan's arrival. Karadzic doesn't admit it. Arkan said he came at the written invitation of Karadzic, but when we expelled him from Bosnia-Herzegovina, two days later he was given a sending-off ceremony by the president, by the supreme commander with various decorations and commendation, et cetera. The same president who never found the time to inspect a single one of our brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, you perhaps more than any other person in this courtroom is familiar with General Mladic's writing and his way of conveying information. Can you help us, when he says he gave 300 of his men, are you able to tell us who is the "he" that Mladic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This says literally Jovica ST, must be Stanisic, is a bit angry. In brackets, he provided 300 men, and now there's a grudge against us that we had advertised Arkan. I cannot draw any conclusion from this sentence. This seems to mean that those 300 men were provided by Jovica Stanisic and that Arkan showed up and he commanded those people and we are giving high profile to Arkan instead of Jovica Stanisic. I don't know that any policeman had come. I'm telling you again, but I know that Arkan came with 300 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we look at just one other entry. It's from the very next day, and it's P2545. And it's a meeting of the 30th of September, 1995. And the J number is J000-0939.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again could I ask you to read this entry before I ask you any questions.
