In this -- in this -- this entry from the notebook it records General Perisic as saying: "Come on, Jovica, let's see what steps can be taken to have some more crossover and to burn that thing." Can you assist us given your knowledge about the time and what was taking place at that time, what is "burn that thing" a reference to, if you know? If you are unable to assist, just please indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't assist either you or myself. How can I know what Perisic meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm looking at this document, also looking at the translation. Now, I remember that there was once an issue about had embedded himself or was embedded. Now, my recollection doesn't go so far that whether it was this portion or not. If it was this portion, then, of course, we should use the new agreed translation, I would think. That's one. And if it's a different portion, then I think there would be a reason to carefully verify the translation here. That came to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, your memory is very accurate. A note has just been handed to me that this is the old translation, not the corrected one. I will not ask about that and I will see that the correct version ...[overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I saw that it was on our screen and, therefore, I'm very much inclined to seek the highest level of precision. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the entry goes on and records a Jovica as saying: "There is no command there, political conflicts, cities are falling...," and it continues. Can you assist us with the following: What location is a person by the name of Jovica referring to as having no command and where cities are falling, again based on your understanding of what was taking place at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, that is just an invitation to speculate. I mean, how could the witness possibly know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask him whether he knows, and if he says he knows what the source of his knowledge is. Any clue, Mr. Milovanovic, that if Jovica says there's no command there that you would know to what location or area he referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is Jovica Stanisic, in fact, it doesn't matter which Jovica it is, this man is right. The period concerned is the time of the defence operation of Republika Srpska against the Croatian Operation Storm. After the fall of Glamoc and Knin, cities continue falling one after another, Drvar, Kljuc, Petrovac, Sanski Most. Fighting is going on for Novi Grad which is mentioned here. There's fighting close to Manjaca and the Ugar River. The command of the 1st Krajina Corps is practically out of operation. Whoever said this is completely right. The command of operative levels from corps down is devastated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether he is right or not wasn't the question. The question was whether you could shed any light on what the their would have been, and what you've told us now is that on the basis of your knowledge on what happened in late September 1995, that an absence of any command you knew that there was in the area that you described, and that for that reason you consider it a possibility that the person, reported to be speaking here, referred to that same area, that's more or less what I understand your testimony to be; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Briefly it's the area of Novi Grad and Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And we have the basis now, Mr. Jordash, because you were concerned about speculation. I think we have the basis for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what the witness doesn't exclude as being referred to. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask the Court Officer to call up to our screens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, I would have one additional question. Mr. Milovanovic, looking at the time-frame and looking at the text, Jovica saying we sent 400 people. Now, you earlier said what the MUP people offered, that was an offer which never materialised, do you have any explanation because it seems here, as Jovica is saying, that they sent 400 people and that it helped at Sanski Most and in Novi Grad. You said this offer from the Serbian MUP officials, well, that was the last thing you heard about it and then we have other information about 300 of Arkan's Men arriving. But here Jovica says: We sent 400 people and the comment is such that it could be interpreted as they were really sent and had arrived because otherwise you would not say that it helped at Sanski Most and Novi Grad. Could you shed any further light on an offer without any follow-up and now a report of an arrival of 400 men by a person Jovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I believe I said I don't know that they ever arrived. I never saw them. And these 400 men mentioned by this Jovica, I never saw them. But he, himself, mentions the areas of Sanski Most and Novi Grad. Nobody was able to help Sanski Most. It fell. But we managed to keep Novi Grad. Twelve days before this Kozarska Dubica was attacked by the regular Croatian army, and the whole conglomerate was made in the Western Krajina and the whole purpose of the Croats was to take Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I'm re-reading your answer on previous questions, but please proceed meanwhile, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving to a different area but I'm happy to return to it if the Chamber would like any assistance in exploring it further. Can I now ask that 65 ter 5603 be brought to our screens. If we could go to e-court page 256 in the original and the English, and it is J000-4671.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, yesterday at transcript page 15416, you were shown an entry from this notebook at e-court pages 253 and 254. The original pages being J000-4672 and J000-4673. This was an entry from a meeting on the 7th of December 1992 with the leadership of Bosanski Samac. I would like to show you a page not shown to you by Mr. Jordash from the same entry, the same meeting. On the page before you Stevan Todorovic states, quote -- Sorry, I don't believe we have it yet, do we?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We need the e-court page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My records indicate e-court page 256. And we are looking at it on our internal systems on that e-court page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could just take the witness back. Earlier you said, Mr. Milovanovic, you thought these were all MUP people and that they should get in touch with the MUP, although the notebook says that they should be incorporated not in the MUP but in a -- forgive me what unit was mentioned, but clearly military unit, and then you say: "I don't know anything else about those police officers. I don't think that they ever arrived." And then you moved on discussing Arkan. That thought, that they never arrived, was that based on anything specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that before I saw this transcript and the words of this Jovica. I said I don't know whether they ever came. Now, I see this Jovica claims they did and I have no reason to disbelieve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, that's not what you said. You are now rephrasing your previous answer: "I said I don't know whether they ever came." What you said is "I don't think that they ever arrived," which is not the same, and you are aware of that, I take it? The one is a thought that something did not happen; the other is a thought that you do not know whether something happened. Are you aware of the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am. When I was talking a moment ago, I said, according to your version, that I think they never arrived. But a couple of minutes later, I saw on the screen a confirmation by some Jovica that they did arrive, so I have to change my opinion. A few minutes ago I thought that they had never arrived but now when I see this on paper I have to change my view, and I believe that they did, they must have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you give us, then, perhaps -- at this second entry, Jovica also says that I think there were -- let me try to find that again. Yes, that it helped at Sanski Most and Novi Grad. What happened in Sanski Most and Novi Grad where the 400 people sent could have helped at that point in time? Was that combat? Was that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Sanski Most and Novi Grad were attacked. Novi Grad was preserved. The attacked was repelled, but Sanski Most fell. We lost it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And in view of the fact that the offer was to incorporate them in a certain unit of the army, do you understand the reference to Sanski Most and Novi Grad as having been helpful in the military operations in those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Those 400 men were probably meant to reinforce one of the VRS units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question with respect to your answers to the Judge Orie's questions. But while I'm asking that question, could I ask the two documents on the screen, could we reverse one page on each one. Could we go to the page before the ones that we see on the screen. The entry begins at the bottom -- or the portion I want to work with begins at the bottom of the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if you would then allow me already one additional question. The operations in relation to Sanski Most and Novi Grad, was the 1st Krajina Corps involved in those operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 1st Krajina Corps with one staff unit, that is the protection regiment, because after Sanski Most the 1st Krajina Corps ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, having listened to you answer the questions of Judge Orie, can we take from this that it is possible that at this time you were not fully aware of the full involvement of Serbian MUP personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I wasn't aware of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we could now turn our attention to 65 ter 5603, and I apologise to the Court Officer for some of the confusion. The B/C/S, the original, was correct that just disappeared from our screen. If we could return that. And with respect to the English, it's e-court page 256. So it's B/C/S e-court page 264 and English e-court 256.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, General, I want to focus on the entry beginning with Mladic recording what Stevan Todorovic, the police chief of Bosanski Samac, said. If you could read that short bit. When you have, indicate so and I will advance to the next page. Now, on this page we are now looking at e-court in the original 265 and in the English 257. Stevan Todorovic is recorded as having said: "Sent 18 men to Ilok for training, and on 18 April 1992, they were transferred in three helicopters together with 30 volunteers from Kragujevac, among them two members of the Serbian MUP, Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, and Aleksandar Vukovic." Do you have any direct knowledge about the transfer of Dragan Djordjevic and Aleksandar Vukovic in three helicopters around this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you be able to assist us in identifying what helicopters might have been used? Would VRS helicopters have been used or possibly used for such a task?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me the date. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is -- talking about the 18th of April, 1992, so mid-April 1992, the transport of 30 volunteers and several others in three helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not have been helicopters of the VRS because at that time we had neither an army nor helicopters. JNA were still ruling in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, before -- this is the last unadmitted Mladic notebook entry that I'm going to work with today. Mr. -- or both Defence teams have tendered the entire series of notebooks. I know that is a matter we'll discuss later, but I do want to note that the Prosecution is interested in tendering this particular excerpt and we'll raise it when we discuss the matter in full. Could I ask that we go now to P2533 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2433"]. It's a notebook entry, the 19th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Perhaps I am a bit late with this. In the previous document there's reference to General Bojic, but I believe that is a translation error. I think it's General Bajic, but we can check that later. It's the previous document we looked at. Page 1, it says "General Bojic," I think it's in fact a reference to General Bajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the impact would be but if the parties could agree on what person a reference to made to, then of course the Chamber would consider that, and it might lead to a correction of the transcript and the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I just inquire whether Mr. Petrovic thinks it would be helpful to have a person who is familiar with General Mladic's handwriting look at and see -- look at the particular page and see whether he can decipher it, or is it simple a matter of translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it could be helpful. The suggestion of my learned friend Mr. Groome is very constructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we return to 65 ter 5603. I understood from Mr. Petrovic's intervention that it was on the first page, if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, you've been listening to Mr. Petrovic question the name of one of the generals, perhaps it's a general that you know. Can you see, can you find it on the first page of 65 ter 5603 and tell us what the correct version of this person's name is, if you can tell. Sorry that's the first page that I called up which is B/C/S -- e-court 264.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to be looking under Stevan Todorovic or a bit further up?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the bottom of the page in B/C/S under the name Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that he was an air force general. His name was Bajic, Ljubomir Bajic. This has to do with helicopters and aircraft. As far as I know, Bajic was the commander of the air force corps in Banja Luka and then after the war he was commander, no, he wasn't the air force commander. In any case, he was connected with the air force. I used to know a General Bojic who served in Kosovo and he became general just before retirement. He was an infantry man, therefore he didn't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can I take it, based on your experience, the name Bojic, which we see on e-court page 256 in the English and 264 in the original, you believe it to be Bajic, B-a-j-i-c; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock. Time for a break unless ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm very near -- I'm at the very end, but I do have a two-minute audiotape to play and another document to bring up. So I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It probably makes sense, I think I will be finished within the first ten minutes of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we take a break. We resume at 25 minutes to 1.00, and then we expect you then to finish within the 15 minutes after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, over the break I was reviewing your evidence this morning, and there was one question that I had posed that you hadn't given a complete answer to. I'd like to pose the question to you again. It was at transcript 29 today. It was when we were talking about communications of the Main Staff. And my question was: When you use the word communication, do you mean to include both reports coming into the Main Staff and directives or orders going out of the Main Staff to subordinate units? In your answer you began to describe some of the technical means for disseminating information or communications. Can I ask you to focus on the part of the question, when you use the word "communication," do you mean both reports coming in and directives and orders going out or one or the other?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. It was two-way communication. Our subordinates reported to us and we communicated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to P2533. It's the last notebook entry that I will work with you during your evidence. It's an entry dated the 19 of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that's being called up, yesterday at transcript 15369, Mr. Jordash asked you about where Mauzer might have gotten supplies from, and you did not have information about that, didn't know. I want to show you this entry and see whether it refreshes your recollection about Mauzer and his relationship with other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we focus on the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And right next to the number 1 is roughly where I would ask you to begin reading. Now, here we see in this entry of the 19th of December, 1993, Mladic list the names of four people, Predrag Jesuric, Savo Kojic, Mauzer, and Dragan Micic. And immediately afterwards he makes the observation: "They have had strong contacts with Serbia's SDB until very recently." Based on your knowledge and work with General Mladic, can you assist us in understanding what he means by this sentence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what General Mladic meant. General Mladic arrived from Knin long before me, I, myself, arrived only on the 11th of May, when everything was already over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Having read this entry does it refresh your recollection to any additional evidence you may possess with respect to who Mauzer may have had relationships with?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunate I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The last thing I want to ask you about in your evidence today is about the tape that you are asked to listen to last evening. Now, the government of Serbia provided the Office of the Prosecutor not only with notebooks but with audiotapes recovered from the Mladic home. The ERN of the number of the tape that you listened to yesterday was T001-2432.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I see Mr. Jordash has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I have an objection to the use of the fresh evidence. Number one, it is new evidence. Number two, it doesn't arise through re-examination. Dealing with the first point, it's new evidence which the Prosecution should have led during their case. It will require -- will prejudice the Defence and will require investigation. And the investigation that it will require will be close examination of this tape, and at the moment the transcript says the speakers are unidentified. I know Mr. Groome wants to ask Mr. Milovanovic to identify the speakers which will then give rise to all manner of investigations which include tracking down those who allegedly are speaking on the tape and ascertaining exactly who they are and trying to meet whatever point my learned friend wants to make about this tape. This at the end of the Stanisic Defence case. In relation to not arising during re-examination did not touch upon anything to do with supplies of Pauk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, but first perhaps, Mr. Petrovic, do you take the same position as Mr. Jordash or would you like to add ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before I deal with the objection, can I just note for the record at page 57.4 it lists the previous exhibit that I worked with as "2433." It is "P2533." So in order to avoid confusion. Your Honour, during Mr. Jordash's examination of this witness he spent some substantial time on pointing out that there was no entry in the diaries of Mr. Stanisic until the 2nd of July, 1993, and then he asked questions about was he -- was it a topic -- was Mr. Stanisic a topic that was discussed at the Main Staff. So I don't prejudice the witness's evidence but perhaps it might be more prudent to ask the witness to remove his head set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite you to take off your earphones for a moment, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I selected this particular audiotape of the many audiotapes recovered from the home for the following reason, and I would note that this audiotape was on our 65 ter list: In it we hear a conversation between Mladic and other people, and it is true that we -- there are -- they have not been fully identified. But throughout that conversation that are several references to Jovica Stanisic. There is a discussion between Mr. General Mladic and others about Jovica Stanisic. This directly contravenes the assertion put to the witness by Mr. Jordash that he was not a topic of discussion with General Mladic. I also note that there are several references to Manojlo, and as the Chamber knows that is the witness's first name. It's perhaps likely that the witness will recognise that this is a conversation that he is aware of. He possibly could be one of the speakers, but certainly for the simple reason that Mr. Stanisic is mentioned by name several times in a discussion held by General Mladic and tape recorded by General Mladic is a basis for asking the witness questions about it. I would also point out, Your Honour, it's on the Defence 65 ter list as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would only add if it was on the Prosecution's 65 ter list then they had it in their possession and ought to have used it at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is not an answer to that the questions are triggered by what you addressed during your further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, my learned friends has rightly put it that I suggested that Mr. Stanisic wasn't a subject of conversation in the years before his first appearance with Mladic on the 2nd of July, 1993. This transcript isn't dated but I'm pretty sure it's 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's still -- we don't know the date. The witness may be able to assist us. I believe it's still relevant for the reasons that I have stated. I do want to correct some misinformation I provided. The audiotape is not on our 65 ter list, it is on the Stanisic Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And why was it not on your 65 ter list, is that to do anything with the availability of the material when you drafted your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I suspect that it has something to do with it, Your Honour, but when the Chamber sees the contents of the audio, there's not all that much relevant information in it. So it's not that the substance is what is relevant or what is being advanced, it's simply the fact that Mr. Stanisic is being discussed by General Mladic and possibly other members of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. One second, Mr. ... so you would say it's not primarily the -- until the 2nd of July but rather whether Mr. Stanisic was a topic that was discussed irrespective of whether it was before or after the first entry in the written notebooks on the 2nd of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd have to go back and check exactly the question that Mr. Jordash put to the witness but I have a distinct memory of the witness being rather emphatic that Mr. Stanisic was not someone who was discussed among members of the Main Staff and I understood his answer to be rather broad in temporal scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us some guidances. What is the portion of -- was it the 6th or the 7th?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe -- one second, Your Honour. I have it in reference to another question. It's at transcript 15436, which I believe was yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that in e-court my 6th of December transcript has not been replaced by the definitely one. Do you have one or two words which would allow me to find the relevant place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Your Honour, uses -- I'll read the passage. It was the question that you had asked, actually. It said: "Judge Orie: The question was whether Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Stanisic's co-operation with the VRS, whether that was something discussed at meetings of the Main Staff. That was the question or was it not." And the answer was: "There was never any discussion about Jovica Stanisic as chief of the State Security of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the problem is if I try to find "co-operation" in my WordWheel, it doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you WordWheel "irregularly," that's three lines above it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are still talking about the 6th or about the 7th?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is the 7th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 7th, yeah, then it's not a surprise that I don't find anything on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So i-r-r-e-g should bring this up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first get the transcript of the 7th on my screen. Yes. It's at page 33 of the old version. The objection is denied. The basis in the answers of the witness gave in cross-examination is sufficient to allow the Prosecution to proceed. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, last evening you were asked to listen to an audio recording. It was ERN number T001-2432. A portion of that audio recording has already been introduced into evidence as P2956. My first question to you regarding that audio is: Did you have an opportunity to listen to it before today?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm inquiring now is whether the technical equipment worked and were you able to listen to it yesterday evening?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to it, but I would like to know from you whether the contents of the tape are the same as the contents of the transcript that you provided me with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A transcriber has listened to the tape and done what they believe to be their best job at recording what was said. Do you ask that because you notice that there were some important differences, or important omissions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I simply noticed that my name was mentioned in a different number of times. At place it was mentioned 17 times and at other places more times. However, the contents of the conversation between Mladic and the person, the unknown person, what I could hear and what was described is pretty much the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you saying now that your name was -- appeared in the transcript at a time when you could not hear it on the audiotape?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. It seems that the person who transcribed the conversation had better listening conditions available to him so he could hear the tape much better than I did. And that's why I asked you whether the contents are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. Mr. Groome, do you want to deal with the whole of the audio or with specific portions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Going to ask some general questions about the time and the participants and then I just have a 2 minute 30 second portion I want to ask specific questions about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we've heard from the witness that, here and there, the transcript, as far as his own name is concerned, might not be -- might even be more complete as he was able to verify in the audio. If this affects in any way your answer to one of the questions that will be put to you by Mr. Groome, Mr. Milovanovic, please don't hesitate to address that matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just inform the court that the transcriber would have used professional equipment and the that copy Mr. Milovanovic listened to was on a Dictaphone, obviously of less quality. That may account for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any continuing disputes about this, I take it that the parties will address that. Again, if it affects one of your answers, please let us know, otherwise just answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, despite the diminished quality of the audio, were you able to recognise the speakers on the tape?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the tape I recognised Mladic's voice at the end because it seems Mladic was recording and he was aware he was recording, so he was talking in a whisper and only in the end he must have lost it and started speaking more loudly, so I recognised his voice. The other person, however, the other speaker, I couldn't recognise the voice but his speech is characterised by volubility and plenty of profanity. The man doesn't take a breath, talks all the time, and there's something in what he says that makes me think it was the time of the counter-strike against Bihac, and there are several indices that indicates it might be a person who was in the government of Vojvodina who might have been deputy speaker of the Assembly or vice-deputy prime minister. I think his last name is Stupar. He came to see me twice in the area of Grmec. And I inferred that from the fact that he tells Mladic is he a native of Bosanski Petrovac. He talks about oil. Now, I don't know whether he was donating oil or trading in oil but proof of that is that he says to Mladic that Milovanovic is taking one-third -- sorry, not Milovanovic, but Manojlo, out of 12 cisterns 4 go to Manojlo, and he will distribute 5.000 to municipalities each. I don't know whether it's 5.000 Deutschemark or 5.000 litres of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a rather long tape and if I could just focus on just a couple of portions and ask your comment on. The references to a Manojlo, do you believe them to be actually references to you or another person with the same name?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it concerns me because he is praising me to Mladic saying that I'm a genius, that the troops love me, they obey me and he asks Mladic at the end: How long till you get into Bihac, will it be just a day or two? And that's how I inferred it must be the Bihac operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've referred or you have placed it in the time-period of the Bihac operation. So the record is clear, can you give us the approximate months and years that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the counter-attack at Bihac from 31st October, 1994, until Carter's truce in -- on 24th December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask now that Mr. Laugel play -- first of all, can we maybe bring to the screens the transcript. It's 65 ter 06330.1. Copy of this 2 minute 30 second portion has been provided to the booths. General, I'm going to play just a short portion of that and then ask you a question afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we have not -- we've not followed the usual procedure which is that we receive an English translation. Therefore, at the English transcript nothing now appears. At the same time, of course, we have on the -- we have a transcript as part of the -- of what I take it you'll tender as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, can the parties live with that, that we have a written -- the problem is that not all parts are well audible. I noticed that there is a French translation, so the French transcript is complete. That's why we had to wait for awhile to have it finished. At this moment also looking at the clock, could the parties agree that we work on the basis of the transcript which then should be also in written form and not only as part of the video be filed as an annex to what may become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the other parties. No one disagrees, although I usually prefer to have a full English transcript. I see that we can live with it for the time being. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, the reference in there about you getting four of something and Jovica Stanisic getting eight of something, is that a reference to the cisterns of fuel that you've referred to just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, these are cisterns of fuel. I don't know about Jovica, I didn't even notice that. I believe I should explain what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's not all that important to us at the moment about whether what those cisterns were. My question actually was going to be something else. Near the beginning of that excerpt we hear one of the speaker say "Jovica will come with his men," and my question is: Do you know what that is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is meant. Jovica never came to see me at Grmec. I found Jovica on the 8th of November at Slunj, that's the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the audio also records a comment about coming from Mirkovci. Does that sound familiar to you, do you recognise that name, and, if so, what can you tell us about Mirkovci?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirkovci is a village near Eastern Slavonia, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us how far it is from another village by the name of Djeletovci, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I don't know where either is but I know they are in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions at this time, Your Honour. There are two things that I would -- three things. One is the Prosecution would tender that excerpt, that's 65 ter 6330.1, and, again, I note that another excerpt is in evidence as P2956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections in addition to what was said already to the use of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Same objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think the ruling on the Prosecution being allowed to use the document also answers the question about admission. Madam Registrar the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P3052, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Groome, would you take care that there is a written -- that is not part of the video, but a written transcript as part of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe it may already be uploaded, but I will check with Mr. Laugel to verify that. And the second matter, Your Honour, is, if I could ask Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness has got his hand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes, before I proceed with that, Mr. Milovanovic, is there a matter you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I don't want the record to remain as it is because I don't know whether this man was smuggling or trading in oil, and I don't want to appear on the record as his accomplice. I had authorisation from the Supreme Command to approve exemptions from customs tax to private oil dealers with the proviso that the army keeps one-third. So out of these 12 cisterns of fuel, four remained for the VRS, not for myself. That's the correction I wanted to make and I don't know if this is the end of my testimony, but I have a question to the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not the end yet of your examination. Witnesses usually are not supposed to ask questions, but we'll later hear from you because the examination of a witness is, as a matter of principle, is a one-way traffic, but we'll see what you'd like to ask to the Defence and then we'll decide whether this is a question appropriately be put to the Defence. Mr. Groome, I think first we should -- yes, admission into evidence has been decided. There was a second matter you would like to I raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, also to make clear in light of the witness's comment, the Prosecution has not presented that tape as any -- with any suggestion that General Milovanovic has done anything incorrect and is in possession of no evidence that anything in that tape was incorrect. Now, with respect to the second matter, Your Honour, the there have been many references to notebook entries over the course of the past three days. If I could ask Madam Registrar to pass up to the Chamber the printed sheet that I provided earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I am sorry to leap to my feet, it's just that I'm noticing the time and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is a matter which can wait until we have excused the witness, Mr. Groome, then I would prefer to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It can, Your Honour, I'm wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then any further questions, it will be you first, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and I fear that I may not finish because Mr. Groome has opened up the whole of the Sanski Most crime base which I need to deal with. In effect, it's a de facto opening of the Prosecution case on this issue, so I would like a little time to deal with that. In addition, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should try to finish. I don't know whether Mr. Petrovic has any specific matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not at this moment but I'm trying to locate a reference, and if I do I may have a few questions to put to the witness with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, try to finish within the time available. And be focused. I have commented quite a couple of times, both Defence teams, on being focused on matters in dispute that took altogether six hours. Let's try to see where we can come.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen please P2546.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to return to the issue of Sanski Most, Mr. Milovanovic. It's a Mladic notebook dated the 3rd of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I want English page 1 and English page -- B/C/S -- sorry, B/C/S page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, we went through -- or you went through with Mr. Groome a number of entries in Sanski Most, but you didn't go through perhaps one that might have assisted you. In fact, there's two or three which I want to remind you of to see if it helps with your recollection of events in Sanski Most. First of all, this one which appears to be a meeting with Filipovic, aka Fica, and Bozovic. Please take a moment to read.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know that Filipovic was suggesting that Arkan was under the control of Pecanac at the beginning of October 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were close to each other. I saw it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did you see to indicate that they were close?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them together at an observation post near Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to the comment which seems to be attributed to Bozovic, or the comments that he was from General Bozovic's house and they had been given a task to replace the RS police who would then go to the forward defence line and its suggested by Mladic there that this was agreed with Karadzic and yourself. Do you know anything about that? Does that trigger your memory about what Bozovic and the Serbian MUP were supposed to be doing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozovic and Filipovic came to see me together, and that was my only meeting with Bozovic. As I have already told you, I don't know. I was not even sure that they ever came back. I never saw Bozovic again at the command of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you don't know whether there was an agreement between Karadzic and Bozovic that the Serbian MUP would replace the RS MUP so that the RS MUP could go into combat?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the first break I said that Karadzic told me that people would arrive from the MUP of Serbia, and indeed Filipovic and Bozovic did arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, when you were being questioned by Mr. Groome and the learned Judge, you indicated that you thought that probably the Serbian MUP had been in combat in a couple of towns. Am I correct though that you don't recall them forming part of the 1st Krajina Corps? You didn't issue any instructions or orders in relation to them or see them in combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that question has been clearly answered already by the witness, isn't it, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 5611, please. It's page 91 of the English, 100 of the original scanned version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we are moving forward from the beginning of October to the 15th of October, 1995, and a meeting with security organs at 12.30. This was not shown to you, so take a moment to read it. You there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I can actually discern is Pero Jakovljevic. I see a reference to Arkan, but I really can't make out head or tail of the whole thing. I'm maybe tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think let's have the typed copy, if we can, please, of the B/C/S which I think is page 91.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not waste time. I can read some things. Yes, but can this be zoomed in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know this Colonel Jakovljevic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. He was the head of the 410th Security Centre and the security organ. He died a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know that he as a security organ was querying along with others who had brought Arkan in the middle of October?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that early this morning. Everybody in the military wondered that and I'm still wondering to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, and you said you wanted to take that up with Karadzic. So am I correct then it follows, doesn't it, that --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It follows, doesn't it that no one in the military was connecting Arkan with the Serbian DB, everyone was querying, and for you, you want to take up the issue with Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I requested those meetings that I already spoke about when the meeting did take place he -- Arkan said that he had an order from the Supreme Command. I asked him to fetch that order but then he changed his mind and he said that he did not have any orders, and then I asked Karadzic before the entire Supreme Command: Plavsic, Koljevic, Krajisnik. And there were three generals: Talic, Koljevic and myself. And Karadzic didn't say a word. And then two days later I saw him being escorted from Bijeljina. I still have my doubts about Karadzic having invited him. He did not engage immediately but he started being violent towards the officers of the Army of Republika Srpska, and then I concluded and I said that to Karadzic that Arkan came to discipline the Army of Republika Srpska. They were after the former soldiers of the Republic of Serbian Krajina who were fleeing across our territory and when they caught them they would detain them at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Looking at the entry: "At the Assembly that they will demand that you are replaced, that Talic take over the Main Staff and Arkan or Lisica take over the 1st Krajina Corps." Were you aware of this news or these rumours that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first ask who "you" is in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who do you think "you" is in this context?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jakovljevic reported to Mladic, so it is Mladic who was supposed to be replaced. All that came to a head once on the 4th of August, 1995, after the fall of Knin. All the generals of the Army of Republika Srpska wrote to the Assembly to overturn that decision. According to that decision, I was supposed to take over the leadership of the army and Mladic was supposed to be appointed as a special advisor, but the generals rejected the decision of the Supreme Command, and the Assembly was in favour of the generals and Mladic was not replaced. Here a security officer reports to Mladic there's something brewing again about his replacement. Talic was supposed to be the head of the General Staff. General Lisica was supposed to be appointed as chief of the 1st Krajina Corps but he was then pensioned off in 1994. I would say that this is a bit far-fetched on the part of the security organ. Talic was my senior in terms of rank, the senior -- than me, so it would only have been logical for him to replace Mladic, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Certainly at this point in time there was open conflicts between Karadzic and Mladic with Karadzic wanting to get rid of Mladic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were never open conflicts between Karadzic and Mladic. Nothing was displayed at meetings. I don't know what happened behind closed doors. However, there was a conflicts between the views of the military and the representatives of politicians. Karadzic represented politicians, Mladic represented the military, and there were conflicts in terms of how to wage that war in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to 65 ter 5611. Page 111. Page 120. And we are moving forward to the 25th of October, Banja Luka, a meeting of the inner circle of the General Staff of the VRS and the commanders on the western part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm interested in the entry which is the first item and what you are purported to have said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please switch off his microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, my concentration fails me here. I can't read the handwriting. The only thing I can see here is that I'm complaining that nothing has arrived from Serbia but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen, please, the typed copy, which is 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it's important that you see it and read it to remind yourself since it's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you say that the Serbian MUP has probably put the border under its control after Arkan was chased away?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see here that for four days there have been no flows of people and goods across the border. This made me conclude that the Serbian MUP closed the border because we had chased Arkan away. But that was not the biggest problem. The biggest problem was our own police, the police of Republika Srpska, after Arkan was chased away. Tomo Kovac did not accept our order on the use of the military police there. We wanted to use the military police on border crossings and there was a deterioration after an RS delegation visited Milosevic which means that somebody from the sphere of politics went to see Milosevic to talk to him about something because Mladic and I were the ones who were behind the decision to chase Arkan away. That night when I had the meeting with Arkan and it was agreed that I would chase him away from Manjaca and Mladic would chase him away from Kotorsko village near Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you presuming the Serbian MUP had put the border under control to keep Arkan out of the region, out of Banja Luka? Is that what you were saying there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I realised then and there at that meeting that the Serbian MUP closed the border for the traffic of people and goods, which means that we couldn't receive anything from them and send anything to them. I know that the generals and politicians could not move across the borders. There was a ban on their travels.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. And Tomo Kovac was not pleased about Arkan being chased away, is that what we should take from this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomo Kovac was angry with the army for having chased the army away which means that Arkan was under the patronage of the MUP of Republika Srpska, and it was well known who was in command of the Republika Srpska MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If there had been Serbian police officers in towns carrying out crime prevention activities, would you necessarily have known that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not have known. All I cared about was warfare and those were not just ordinary policemen but special police officers, those who could be and were engaged in combat. I was not interested in public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it ever reported to you that Stanisic had said that Arkan had embedded himself in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me that. The only thing I found out was that Arkan had a room at the hotel Bosna, whereas his mob was scattered all over Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to refer to P61 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a different subject. It's the subject of airfields and combat flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And could we have, please, page 11 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, while that is coming up, Mr. Milovanovic, this is a speech that Mr. Groome referred to, a speech by Mr. Simatovic, and I want to make sure that you understand what was actually being suggested by Simatovic and ask you to comment on it, please. I want to focus on the section which begins, I think, actually, we need to go to the B/C/S page 9 because I'm going to deal with the airfields point first. And I want to deal with the claim that in 1992 they, i.e., the Serbian DB, began building and securing a network of small airfields in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also forming a combat squadron. If you would read that, please. And if you would read down to the sentence just before the sentence dealing with the Captain Dragan's Fund.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that page in front of me in B/C/S. Stop. No, no. I can see that, actually, but the counsel mentioned the year 1991, so shall I read the portion starting with the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Also in 1992," start with that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is reading, how much time would you still need, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I could -- well, I don't know what the witness is going to -- I want to take him through just some small sections on this speech which will take about 10 minutes, and then the problem is I would also like to take him into the subject of this audiotape and I don't know what he is going to say because I have no idea what it all means. So I think maybe 30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, five minutes, let's say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As matter stands now, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read the entire text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The total of the time still needed would amount to approximately 20 to 25 minutes, and where otherwise would have to keep the witness here until Tuesday afternoon, I am just looking at the possibility and I first have to confer with my colleagues whether we could extend this session with some 20 to 25 minutes, and then I would be very strict on timing and I add to this that if the time used during the first six hours of examination would have been used more focused then we would have avoided this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if we get the approval of all those assisting us, and I'm not the master of their time, then you would have from now on exactly 17 minutes which brings us to three minutes past 2.00, then five minutes for Mr. Petrovic and that would be it. Mr. Groome, as matters stand now, of course then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I just ask that we go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And may I take it that you have verified with support staff and officials. We provisionally proceed on this basis and if there are major -- if there's major opposition we would hear that. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm very grateful to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You, in response to questions from Mr. Groome, who put to you a part of what Mr. Simatovic had said, you said "as for auxiliary airfields where airfields can take off and land," apart from the four that you mentioned in your testimony," I don't know any others because we didn't use them and there was no need for me to be interested in them." And I want to ask you, therefore, about what Mr. Simatovic said. Did you observe at any point a network of small airfields being run by the Serbian DB in VRS territory during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Given the equipment and surveillance units you had under your subordination, do you think you would have noticed a network of small airfields and the DB running thousands, or hundreds even, combat, humanitarian, reconnaissance, and transport flights?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been impossible for anybody to be flying apart from or next to the air force of Republika Srpska because those airports - Sokolac, Rogatica - simply did not exist. The airport I'm talking about, we just marked the air strip, and it has not changed to this day, it is not operational. And in Bratunac, the air strip was a bit longer but it was a macadam air strip so only propellor aircraft could land. We had one of those transport planes -- we had a pet name of it -- for it, Old Vujadin, and that was the only thing that landed. I think it was the AN2 type plane. And as for the other air forces, there were none in Republika Srpska because on the 31st of March, 1993, the no-fly zone resolution of the Security Council was imposed and I'm sure that people from Yugoslavia had not been so crazy as to send their aircraft our way, into the jaws of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise on page 81, line 18 and 19, the witness mentioned another two airfields which did not exist and still they are mentioned in this entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, where you referred to the Bratunac air strip, did you make reference to any other air strips?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned the airfield at Bratunac or in brackets -- Skelani. That's the airport between Bratunac and Skelani. Before the war there was only two municipalities, Bratunac and Srebrenica. Skelani as a municipality did not exist before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you are not invited to repeat your evidence but just say what other air strips you mentioned. Mr. Petrovic, the matter has been -- otherwise you can ask for a correction of the transcript on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... no Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic said that in mid-spring of last year, which would have been 1995, the DB retreated from these parts with complete equipment and machinery, helicopters, and aircraft. Did you observe the Serbian DB doing that, and would you have, if they had?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm totally confused now. What year are we talking about? What speech are you talking about? You are talking about Simatovic's speech from the year 1991 and you put before me some events that took place in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you about a speech which was made in 1996. This speech was made in 1996. And, I beg your pardon, 1997. And I'm asking you whether you saw the DB in -- well, 1996 or 1995 or any year, removing equipment detailed, helicopters and aircraft, and so on, the type of equipment that would be used in an airfield? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What a -- you gave evidence about your helicopter being detected by General Morillon. How often were you using that helicopter before he detected you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What? What happened to my helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You testified, when Mr. Groome was asking you questions, about flying your helicopter and you were never detected until General Morillon complained about it. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used the helicopter whenever I needed. NATO radars could not detect me. Morillon, however, did detect me. I was supposed to meet him between Srebrenica and Bratunac when he had been captured by Naser Oric. I was supposed to be involved in negotiations. I used a helicopter. He asked me how I had arrived. I said I used the helicopter to fly into Bratunac, and then a few days later, he complained before the Security Council that I had used the helicopter and that I violated the no-fly zone agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Morillon or any other international authority from NATO, or otherwise, complain to you about the DB flying with helicopters or aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did any of your security organs report that to you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yugoslav helicopters did not fly over the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was only once that General Perisic flew over the Drina River near the village of whose name I forget now. He entered the Serbian territory in the depth of 50 metres. Milosevic sent him to talk to me and to butter him up so I would be prepared to accept the Contact Group plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. If your security organs had observed that, would you expect them to have put that into written reports?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me try again. If a entity other than the VRS was flying hundreds of flights in VRS territory, supplying military organisations, wouldn't you expect your security organs to record that in one report at least?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The commander of the air force and anti-aircraft defence of the Army of Republika Srpska informed me about that. He would have been the one to brief me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And they didn't, did they?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They informed me regularly about the number of sorties, the type of aircraft when NATO aircraft flew over Bosnia-Herzegovina and especially when they bombarded us. They informed me about all sorts of flights, reconnaissance flights, combat flights and all types of flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Belonging to NATO, but no other entity?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody else flew over Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now just take you to another part of the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go to page 8 of the B/C/S and page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me deal with this more swiftly. Simatovic also claimed that there was -- the DB ran training camps in Banja Luka, Doboj, Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina, Trebinje, Visegrad, Ozren, and Mrkonjic Grad. Did you see them, would you have seen them if they existed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I was in no position to see them from Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm talking about training camps allegedly in existence in -- well, it's unclear, we haven't been given dates, but let's just say 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This speech was delivered in May 1991. And it says that the -- I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The speech was not delivered in May 1991. Did you ever hear of training camps Mr. Simatovic in the speech claimed to exist in Banja Luka, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Doboj? Any in Doboj? Any of the DB-ran training camps in Banja Luka, Doboj, Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina, Trebinje, Visegrad, Ozren and Mrkonjic Grad. Did you ever hear about DB-run training camps between 1992 and 1995 in these places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the State Security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about a training camp in Doboj. I heard that in -- from somebody's testimony, but I don't know when and I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any additional knowledge about this training camp apart from what you heard in someone else's testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Given the resources that would be needed to set up a training base, would you have expected to have seen some trace, the delivery of supplies, the movement of men, and so on, if those training bases had existed and been under the supervision of the DB?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only if I had ventured into the area by chance to see some traces of what, boots or something else? No, I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just deal very quickly with the section of the tape that you listened to. Did you understand what this tape was saying? Did it make sense to you? Did it trigger off any recollections, the tape you listened to overnight?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an insignificant document for me. It may be of some interest for you because one of those men hailed from outside of Serbia. He lives in Novi Sad, to be more specific. He mentions Zeleni, I don't know in what context, I didn't understand that. He was born in Petrovac. I don't know what his purpose was, whether he came back to his -- to the place where he was born, how he was involved in the trade of fuel, I don't know. For me that tape and that document was totally insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever, as far as you know, share supplies with Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Supplies of oil or any other supplies of military type logistics?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have enough to distribute among my men let alone some to Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the answer to the first question was clear: You never shared supplies with Mr. Stanisic. Then to say: Did you never share oil, did you never share vehicles, I mean no supplies and then you start continuing. Okay, that's -- I gave you 17 minutes. You've had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I can't in the time go through this tape, so I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Groome said he was not primarily interested in the contents of the conversation. Mr. Groome, is that correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But I'm not sure that means what that means legally, I mean, not primarily means he will use the contents but it may not be his primary concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic now has an opportunity to put further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just awhile ago you said that it is well known who was in charge of the MUP of Republika Srpska. You didn't give us any names. Who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier today you answered questions about the establishment of a communication system within the Army of Republika Srpska after the 12th of May, 1992. Up to that time was there a communication system established by the Yugoslav People's Army in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it existed and there were 13 hubs that remained in the territory of Republika Srpska. I said earlier today that I inherited all those communication hubs from the war command post from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question, sir. We all spoke at length about those police officers from Serbia who either arrived or did not arrive in Republika Srpska in the autumn of 1995. Let's leave that aside, do you know anything about possible policemen from Serbia possibly be -- having been engaged in combat in Republika Srpska? I'm talking about autumn 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic, for staying within the time-limit. The first question could have easily answered by an agreement. The second question you put to the witness, at least the answer he gave, he gave already earlier. And on the third question we now know that he didn't know anything about it. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Which means...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This means that this concludes your evidence, Mr. Milovanovic. I'd like to thank you very much for not only coming once but even coming a second time. We'll not keep you here until the 20th of December. Instead, we wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher. There was a matter you said at the end you would like to raise, if you can briefly do that, if there's still need. You said you wanted to ask something to the Defence, but first address me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to ask the Defence what to do with the materials that tormented me for three nights? I would love to keep those materials because I'm working on a project and I could use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll receive instructions given by the Defence to the -- on a request of the Defence to the Victims and Witness Section what to do with that material. I'm specifically addressing Mr. Jordash. Any confidentiality matter which may be involved?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll take care of that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you'll receive further information about that, Mr. Milovanovic. Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm wondering whether there's any way to either sit together or deal with the matter of scheduling of next week's witnesses because we have received the Simatovic Defence e-mail of the 6th of December stating that Simatovic Defence witness DFS-001 will be replaced by DFS-014. Is there any way we can deal with that perhaps out side of this setting because the interpreters, technicians, but me, myself, as well we have other hearings this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll send an e-mail informing the Chamber and Defence counsel my position and perhaps we can then formally deal with it first thing Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does that mean that you would oppose replacement because it has a, of course, a very ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can state my position in about 30 seconds, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 seconds would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution is opposing -- does not oppose the rescheduling of the witness, does oppose the Prosecution be required to begin its cross-examination. The witness testified in over nine days, in two cases, over 750 pages of transcript. We don't have any of the exhibits documents translated and the lawyer scheduled to do this cross-examination leaves tomorrow on annual leave. We don't oppose the witness to come begin direct examination. But we will be unable to begin our cross-examination next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was 31 seconds, Mr. Groome, but nevertheless very close to the target. We will adjourn, and I'll apologise to all those who are assisting us giving you perhaps far too heavy burden on your shoulders, but we'll resume Tuesday, the 13th of December, 2011, quarter past 2.00 in this same Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of December, 2011 at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
